love.note: Love is one of Scripture's central threads — God's steadfast love for humanity, the call to love God fully, and the command to love one's neighbor (and even one's enemies). In the New Testament, love (agape) is described as patient, selfless, and active rather than merely emotional (1 Corinthians 13).

faith.note: Faith describes confident trust in God's character and promises, even without full sight of the outcome. Hebrews 11 calls it 'the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen,' and faith is repeatedly linked to how a person is made right with God.

hope.note: Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but a confident expectation grounded in God's promises and character. It anchors believers through hardship, pointing toward future restoration and eternal life.

grace.note: Grace is unearned favor — God's generosity toward people who could not earn or deserve it. It's central to the New Testament understanding of salvation as a gift rather than a reward for good works.

peace.note: Peace (shalom) in Scripture is broader than the absence of conflict — it describes wholeness, right relationship with God, and inner calm that can persist even amid difficulty (Philippians 4:7).

joy.note: Joy is presented as a deep, durable gladness rooted in God rather than circumstances — it's listed as fruit of the Spirit and something believers are repeatedly urged to hold onto, even in suffering.

wisdom.note: Wisdom literature (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Job) frames wisdom as practical, God-honoring skill for living. 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom' recurs as a foundational theme.

strength.note: Strength in Scripture often flips human expectation — it's frequently described as coming through reliance on God rather than self-sufficiency ('when I am weak, then am I strong,' 2 Corinthians 12:10).

healing.note: Healing appears both physically (miracles in the Gospels) and spiritually/emotionally (restoration of relationship with God). It's tied closely to compassion, faith, and God's care for the whole person.

patience.note: Patience is listed among the fruit of the Spirit and is closely tied to love and endurance — the capacity to wait well and respond gently rather than react in anger.

trust.note: Trusting God is presented as an alternative to relying on one's own understanding (Proverbs 3:5-6), especially in times of uncertainty or danger.

courage.note: Courage in Scripture is frequently commanded alongside a reminder of God's presence — 'be strong and of a good courage... for the LORD thy God is with thee' (Joshua 1:9).

mercy.note: Mercy is compassion shown to those in need or fault, often paired with justice. It reflects God's character and is something believers are called to extend to others.

forgiveness.note: Forgiveness is central to the Gospel message — believers are described as forgiven by God and are, in turn, instructed to forgive others, sometimes framed as a condition of receiving forgiveness themselves (Matthew 6:14-15).

sin.note: Sin describes wrongdoing or falling short of God's standard. Scripture presents it as a universal human condition addressed through repentance and, in Christian theology, through the work of Christ.

death.note: Death is treated as both a physical reality and a spiritual concept (separation from God). The New Testament repeatedly contrasts death with the hope of resurrection and eternal life.

life.note: 'Life' spans physical existence and a deeper, abundant spiritual life offered through relationship with God (John 10:10) — often set against death as its opposite.

light.note: Light symbolizes truth, purity, guidance, and God's presence, frequently contrasted with darkness as a metaphor for sin, ignorance, or separation from God.

darkness.note: Darkness often represents sin, evil, confusion, or separation from God's presence, set in contrast to light and truth throughout Scripture.

truth.note: Truth is tied closely to God's character and to Jesus himself ('I am the way, the truth, and the life,' John 14:6), and is presented as something that liberates (John 8:32).

righteousness.note: Righteousness describes right standing with God and right living. The New Testament frames it as both a gift received through faith and a pattern of life to pursue.

kingdom.note: The 'Kingdom of God' or 'Kingdom of Heaven' is a major theme of Jesus's teaching — God's reign breaking into the world, described through parables as something both present and still coming.

spirit.note: The Holy Spirit is presented as God's active presence, empowering, guiding, comforting, and producing spiritual growth ('fruit of the Spirit') in believers.

holy.note: Holiness describes being set apart, pure, and consecrated to God. It's both a description of God's nature and a call for believers to live distinctively.

covenant.note: A covenant is a binding relational agreement — Scripture is structured around a series of covenants (Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the New Covenant) describing God's commitments to his people.

promise.note: God's promises are a recurring anchor throughout Scripture, often given long before their fulfillment, underscoring themes of faithfulness and patient trust.

blessing.note: Blessing describes God's favor and provision, often pronounced over individuals, families, or nations, and sometimes tied to obedience or covenant relationship.

temptation.note: Temptation is the pull toward wrongdoing. Scripture teaches that temptation itself isn't sin, offers examples (including Jesus's own temptation), and promises that God provides a way through it (1 Corinthians 10:13).

obedience.note: Obedience to God is frequently linked to love and trust — 'if ye love me, keep my commandments' (John 14:15) — rather than being framed as mere rule-following.

humility.note: Humility — a modest view of oneself and posture of service — is repeatedly commended, with Jesus's own life held up as the model (Philippians 2:5-8).

pride.note: Pride is generally treated as spiritually dangerous in Scripture — 'pride goeth before destruction' (Proverbs 16:18) — standing in contrast to humility.

gratitude.note: Thankfulness is encouraged as a consistent posture toward God, regardless of circumstance ('in every thing give thanks,' 1 Thessalonians 5:18).

anger.note: Scripture acknowledges anger as a real emotion while repeatedly cautioning against letting it lead to sin ('be ye angry, and sin not,' Ephesians 4:26) and commending a slow-to-anger disposition.

comfort.note: God is described as 'the God of all comfort,' who comforts people in affliction so that they, in turn, can comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:3-4).

marriage.note: Marriage is portrayed as a significant covenant relationship, used at times as an image for God's relationship with his people and for Christ's relationship with the Church.

children.note: Children are described as a blessing and heritage, with instruction given both to children and to parents about how to raise and relate to one another.

work.note: Work is treated as a meaningful part of human life from creation onward, with encouragement to work diligently 'as unto the Lord' rather than merely for human approval.

money.note: Money itself isn't condemned, but the 'love of money' is called 'a root of all kinds of evil' (1 Timothy 6:10). Scripture repeatedly warns against letting wealth become an object of trust or worship.

wealth.note: Wealth is treated with caution — potentially a blessing, but also a spiritual risk if it displaces trust in God or generosity toward others.

poverty.note: Care for the poor is a consistent ethical demand throughout Scripture, tied closely to justice, generosity, and God's own concern for the vulnerable.

justice.note: Justice — fairness, righting wrongs, and caring for the vulnerable — is presented as central to God's character and something his people are called to practice, not merely believe in.

mourning.note: Grief is treated honestly in Scripture (as in the Psalms and Lamentations), with comfort promised to those who mourn (Matthew 5:4) rather than grief being dismissed.

praise.note: Praise — verbal and communal celebration of God's character and acts — runs throughout the Psalms and is presented as a fitting response to who God is.

worship.note: Worship describes reverence and devotion directed to God, encompassing both communal ritual and everyday life ('present your bodies a living sacrifice,' Romans 12:1).

prayer.note: Prayer is presented as ongoing communication with God — including praise, confession, request, and thanksgiving — modeled by Jesus and commanded as a regular practice ('pray without ceasing,' 1 Thessalonians 5:17).

fear.note: Scripture distinguishes between anxious fear (repeatedly countered with 'fear not') and reverent 'fear of the LORD,' a posture of awe described as the beginning of wisdom.

anxiety.note: Believers are repeatedly urged not to be anxious but to bring concerns to God in prayer, with peace promised in return (Philippians 4:6-7; Matthew 6:25-34).

salvation.note: Salvation describes deliverance — ultimately, in Christian theology, rescue from sin and its consequences through faith in Christ — and is a central theme spanning both testaments.

redemption.note: Redemption pictures being 'bought back' from bondage or debt — used both of Israel's deliverance from slavery and, in the New Testament, of deliverance from sin through Christ.

resurrection.note: The resurrection of Jesus is the central claim of the New Testament, presented as the basis for hope in believers' own future bodily resurrection and eternal life.

eternal life.note: Eternal life is described not just as unending existence but as a quality of life in relationship with God, beginning now and continuing beyond physical death.

heaven.note: Heaven is described as God's dwelling and the hope of believers' future, with Revelation depicting a renewed creation ('a new heaven and a new earth') rather than a purely disembodied afterlife.

judgment.note: Judgment refers to God's evaluation of human life and action, described both as a present reality and a future event, closely tied to themes of justice and mercy.

repentance.note: Repentance is a change of mind and direction — turning from sin toward God — presented as the appropriate response to God's grace and a recurring call throughout Scripture.

shepherd.note: Shepherd imagery pictures God's (and later Jesus's) guidance, protection, and provision for his people, most famously in Psalm 23 and John 10 ('I am the good shepherd').

sheep.note: Sheep represent God's people — often depicted as needing guidance and prone to wander — cared for by a shepherd, a metaphor Jesus applies directly to himself and his followers.

cross.note: The cross is the central symbol of Christian faith, representing Jesus's sacrificial death and, in New Testament theology, the means of reconciliation between God and humanity.

blood.note: Blood in Scripture is tied to life, atonement, and covenant — from Old Testament sacrificial systems to the New Testament's description of Christ's blood as securing forgiveness.

temple.note: The temple was the central place of worship and sacrifice in Israel, later reinterpreted in the New Testament as Jesus's body, and then as believers themselves ('ye are the temple of God,' 1 Corinthians 3:16).

prophet.note: Prophets served as messengers who spoke God's word to their communities — often calling for repentance, warning of consequences, and pointing toward future hope.

disciple.note: A disciple is a committed follower and learner. The Gospels describe the cost and shape of discipleship to Jesus, including self-denial and imitation of his life.

gospel.note: 'Gospel' means 'good news' — in the New Testament, specifically the news of Jesus's life, death, and resurrection, and the salvation offered through him.

miracle.note: Miracles in Scripture typically function as signs pointing to God's power and identity, especially in the Gospels where Jesus's miracles are tied to his teaching and identity as Messiah.

freedom.note: Freedom in Scripture often moves beyond physical liberty to spiritual freedom from sin's power ('if the Son... shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed,' John 8:36).

wilderness.note: The wilderness is a recurring setting for testing, provision, and formation — from Israel's forty years to Jesus's own forty days of temptation.

law.note: 'The Law' (Torah) refers to the instructions given through Moses. The New Testament discusses its purpose, its fulfillment in Christ, and its relationship to grace at length, especially in Romans and Galatians.

commandments.note: God's commandments, epitomized by the Ten Commandments, are presented as guidance for life in relationship with God and others, summarized by Jesus as loving God and loving neighbor.

rest.note: Rest (including the Sabbath) is established from creation onward as a rhythm of life, and Jesus offers spiritual rest to those who are weary ('come unto me... and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28).

fruit.note: Fruit is used as a metaphor for the visible outcome of a person's life or spiritual condition — most notably the 'fruit of the Spirit' (Galatians 5:22-23) as evidence of a Spirit-led life.

vine.note: Jesus uses the vine and branches image to describe abiding, dependent connection to him as the source of spiritual fruitfulness (John 15).

angel.note: Angels appear throughout Scripture as messengers and agents of God, often delivering news, providing protection, or executing God's purposes.

satan.note: Satan is portrayed as an adversarial spiritual figure associated with temptation, accusation, and opposition to God's purposes, ultimately depicted as defeated in the biblical narrative's resolution.

servant.note: Servanthood is elevated as a model of greatness in the Kingdom of God, with Jesus himself described as taking 'the form of a servant' (Philippians 2:7) and washing his disciples' feet.

shame.note: Shame is addressed throughout Scripture, often paired with promises of restoration — 'whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed' (Romans 10:11).

loneliness.note: God's presence and companionship are repeatedly offered as an answer to isolation — 'I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee' (Hebrews 13:5).

suffering.note: Suffering is treated honestly rather than explained away — the Psalms and Job wrestle openly with pain, while the New Testament frames some suffering as formative and temporary in light of future hope (Romans 8:18).

endurance.note: Endurance is commended as a quality produced through trials, described as leading toward maturity and a settled hope (James 1:2-4; Romans 5:3-4).

generosity.note: Generosity is repeatedly commended as a reflection of God's own generosity, with 'God loveth a cheerful giver' (2 Corinthians 9:7) capturing the tone of much New Testament teaching on giving.

purity.note: Purity describes moral and spiritual integrity, prized in Scripture ('blessed are the pure in heart,' Matthew 5:8) as reflecting an undivided devotion to God.

glory.note: Glory describes the weight, splendor, and honor of God's presence and character, and is also used of the destiny believers are promised to share in.

creation.note: The creation narrative in Genesis frames the world as intentionally made and declared 'good,' establishing themes of order, purpose, and humanity's role within it that echo through the rest of Scripture.

water.note: Water functions symbolically throughout Scripture — for cleansing, judgment (the flood), deliverance (the Red Sea), and spiritual life ('living water,' John 4:10).

bread.note: Bread represents sustenance and provision, from manna in the wilderness to Jesus describing himself as 'the bread of life' (John 6:35) and instituting the Last Supper.

harvest.note: Harvest imagery describes both literal agricultural provision and spiritual outcomes — the reaping of what is sown, and metaphorically, the gathering of people into God's kingdom.

exile.note: Exile — particularly Israel's exile to Babylon — is a major theme of displacement and discipline, paired with prophetic promises of eventual restoration and return.

promised land.note: The Promised Land represents the fulfillment of God's covenant promise to Abraham's descendants, later used as a picture of rest and inheritance beyond its literal geography.

second coming.note: The return of Christ is presented as the future hope that resolves the biblical story, bringing final judgment, restoration, and the establishment of God's kingdom in full.

end times.note: Passages about the end times (eschatology) describe future events surrounding Christ's return, often symbolically, and are read with a wide range of interpretive approaches across Christian traditions.

sabbath.note: The Sabbath is a day of rest instituted from creation and formalized in the Ten Commandments, later addressed by Jesus as made 'for man' rather than man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

leadership.note: Biblical leadership is repeatedly redefined around service rather than status — 'whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister' (Matthew 20:26).

unity.note: Unity among believers is a major New Testament concern, especially in Paul's letters, picturing the church as one body with many interdependent parts (1 Corinthians 12).

enemies.note: Scripture's teaching on enemies is distinctive — rather than only self-defense or retaliation, believers are instructed to love and pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:44).

wine.note: Wine appears both as a symbol of blessing and celebration (as at the wedding at Cana) and as an image in the Last Supper representing Christ's blood of the new covenant.

lion.note: The lion is used both as an image of danger (1 Peter 5:8) and, notably, of Christ ('the Lion of the tribe of Juda,' Revelation 5:5), symbolizing strength and kingship.

lamb.note: The lamb, especially the Passover lamb, becomes a central image for Christ as 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' (John 1:29), pointing to sacrificial atonement.
